js_003: Who wrote ‘Self-Study Power — the one power we need in the AI age’?
js_008: The author is Ko Yo-el. He majored in business at the National University of Singapore, yet taught himself AI, ended up lecturing, and even won recognition from global companies and the UK government.
js_010: In what age does this book say ‘self-study’ is exactly the power you need?
js_011: An uncertain age where AI is changing everything
js_012: The early industrial age when factories were multiplying
js_013: The age when the internet was just starting to spread
js_014: A bygone age when everyone aimed only at getting into college
js_015: It is exactly the subtitle: ‘the one power we need in the AI age.’ The more common knowledge becomes, the more the power to learn on your own sets people apart, it says.
js_017: Which is closest to what the author means by ‘self-study power’?
js_018: Setting your own purpose and marshalling every means to learn what you need
js_019: Simply following, without ever asking why, a study timetable that someone else drew up for you
js_020: A natural-born knack for memorizing whatever you read at high speed
js_021: Diligently leaning on cram schools and private tutors to be taught
js_022: Self-study bundles a clear purpose + every means + self-driven learning. The author calls it not talent but the power of diligence.
js_024: In the AI age, what does the author say sets people apart instead of ‘credentials’?
js_025: Self-study — the power to keep learning on your own
js_026: The nameplate of which university you graduated from
js_027: The IQ you happened to be assigned at birth
js_028: How wide a network of connections you have built
js_029: The author says ‘the age of credentials is fading and the age of self-study is coming.’ Not a nameplate but the power to learn on your own becomes your edge.
js_031: What ability did the author single out as common to Musk, Gates, and Zuckerberg?
js_032: Self-study that reached beyond the fence of their major
js_033: An elite university diploma that everyone envies
js_034: A huge fortune inherited from wealthy, enviable parents
js_035: A lucky, perfectly-timed moment to start a company
js_036: These world-changing founders taught themselves fields they never studied in school and opened new industries. The author sees self-study as their common thread.
js_038: What common myth about ‘self-study’ does the author correct?
js_039: That you must do it all alone, struggling with no one’s help
js_040: That you should set a clear purpose before you begin to learn
js_041: That being consistent matters more than anything else does
js_042: That you have to produce a tangible result in the end
js_043: Self-study is not ‘studying in isolation.’ Real self-study, the author stresses, mobilizes every means — books, lectures, people, even AI.
js_045: What did the author stress as the ‘very first thing’ to do in self-study?
js_046: Setting a clear purpose — why and what you will learn
js_047: Stocking up on pricey textbooks and courses first
js_048: Cranking your daily study load far above everyone else
js_049: Just copying whatever study everyone else is doing
js_050: If the purpose is blurry, the method wobbles too. Deciding ‘for what, and what’ to learn first is where self-study begins.
js_052: In the definition of self-study, what is the right attitude toward ‘means and methods’?
js_053: Mobilize every means you can — books, lectures, people, AI
js_054: Stubbornly stick to a single paper book and nothing else
js_055: Follow only what school teaches in scheduled class hours
js_056: Never touch a search engine or any other tool at all
js_057: You use anything that helps you reach your purpose. Holding nothing back — total mobilization — is the core attitude of self-study.
js_059: In the end, the author calls self-study ‘the power of what’?
js_060: The power of diligence, seeing it through toward a purpose
js_061: The power of genius that memorizes it all in one look
js_062: The power of last-minute cramming right before a test
js_063: The power of clever little shortcuts and quick tricks
js_064: The author nails it down: self-study is the power of diligence. Not sparkling talent but consistency builds real skill.
js_066: Which approach did the author see as more effective for self-study?
js_067: Building up a little every day, consistently
js_068: Cramming it all in right before the test
js_069: Diving in deep only when you feel like it
js_070: Pushing many times the usual load all at once
js_071: ‘A little every day, consistently’ beats ‘once, short and deep.’ Only repetition makes knowledge truly yours.
js_073: Kyobo Book Centre — ‘Self-Study Power’ book info
js_085: Ko Yo-el was a business student at the National University of Singapore, with no formal training in computer science or AI. By pure self-study he became an AI expert and took the lectern.
js_086: The more AI equalizes access to knowledge, the wider the gap in ‘the power to learn and use it yourself’ grows — that is this book’s central concern.
js_087: Self-study = a clear purpose + every means + self-driven learning. Bundling these three into ‘the power of diligence’ is the heart of this book.
js_088: ‘Credentials (a nameplate)’ barely change once fixed, but ‘self-study’ can grow for a lifetime. That makes it a stronger weapon in an age of change.
js_089: Musk taught himself much of rocket science; Gates and Zuckerberg, much of programming. Their common thread is ‘the power to dig in on your own,’ not their major.
js_090: The myth that ‘self-study means isolation’ wears people out. Asking people and taking lectures are all means of self-study too. It is not about suffering alone.
js_091: If the purpose is vague, you can’t decide what or how much to learn. Only when ‘why you learn’ is clear do the method, amount, and order follow.
js_092: The moment you pick and choose means, learning narrows. Total mobilization means pulling in anything that helps — books, video, people, AI, hands-on practice.
js_093: Why the author calls self-study ‘the power of diligence’ — because it takes not a special mind but ‘the attitude of steadily seeing it through,’ open to anyone.
js_094: ‘A little every day’ wins because of forgetting. Meeting it briefly and often catches it again before it slips, moving it into long-term memory.
js_108: The power to set your own purpose, mobilize every means, and learn what you need on your own initiative. The author calls it ‘the power of diligence.’
js_110: The more AI equalizes access to knowledge, the more the power to learn and use it yourself sets people apart.
js_112: Only when why and what you learn is clear do method, amount, and order follow. A blurry purpose makes self-study wobble.
js_113: A self-check that separates what you know from what you don’t. Clearing away the illusion of knowing lets you fill the gaps precisely.
js_115: If you can’t explain it in plain words, you don’t really know it. Where your explanation stalls is exactly what you don’t understand.
js_117: AI is the flagship tool of total mobilization. Ask well and it’s a 24/7 private tutor; copy only the answers and nothing sticks.
js_119: Input alone never becomes skill. Only by making something — writing, code, a work — does knowledge harden into a usable form.
js_121: The belief that ‘ability grows.’ The attitude that consistency, not talent, builds skill is what sustains self-study.
js_123: How a business student self-taught his way to the AI lectern
js_124: Author Ko Yo-el was a business major who had never formally studied computer science or AI.
js_125: Offered a chance to teach AI, he dug in by self-study alone, took the lectern, and won recognition as an expert.
js_126: The conviction he drew from it — the real weapon of the AI age is not credentials but ‘self-study.’
js_127: The question running through the book: when no one teaches you, can you learn on your own?
js_129: Why ‘self-study’ now — the age of credentials is fading
js_130: The more AI makes knowledge common, the more the power to learn and use it yourself creates the gap.
js_131: A ‘nameplate’ you once earned goes stale fast. In an age of change you must keep updating yourself.
js_132: What Musk, Gates, and Zuckerberg share — they opened industries by self-study, beyond their majors.
js_133: This isn’t about rejecting school — it’s about adding self-study on top of it.
js_135: The myths of self-study, and why studying used to fail
js_136: The myth that ‘self-study means going it alone’ wears you out. People and lectures are means of self-study too.
js_137: Start without a purpose and you lose direction. Study missing the ‘why’ never lasts.
js_138: Weak metacognition traps you in the ‘illusion of knowing,’ so you walk right past what you don’t grasp.
js_139: Repeat only reading and listening (input) and never make anything (output), and skill never sticks.
js_141: How to build self-study — mindset, tactics, and output
js_142: The growth mindset that ‘ability grows’ comes first. It turns failure into material for learning.
js_143: It mobilizes concrete tactics — setting a purpose, good questions, the Feynman technique, AI tutors, verifying information.
js_144: Repeat daily, however small, to build a habit, and push through to the end while managing stress.
js_145: Last comes output — make something from what you learned to prove your skill and fill the gaps.
js_147: A business major, the author had never formally studied AI, yet when offered a chance to teach he dug in by pure self-study and took the lectern. He went on to have his expertise recognized by global companies and the UK government.
js_148: The author himself proves the book’s claim: ‘even outside your major, self-study can carry you to the top.’
js_149: Founders who opened industries outside their majors
js_150: Elon Musk taught himself much of rocket science; Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg, much of programming — and each built a new industry. It was digging-in self-study, more than any degree, that made them.
js_151: A prime example showing that the shared key to success may be ‘self-study,’ not ‘credentials.’
js_152: The AI age, where anyone can have a private tutor
js_153: In the past you needed a good teacher or academy to learn; now you can ask AI, request explanations, and learn on your own. The tool is the same, but the result splits on ‘how you ask and use it.’
js_154: It makes you realize that as opportunity levels out, ‘the power to learn and use it yourself’ becomes the more decisive difference.
js_155: Have I only followed a curriculum others set, or have I ever set my own purpose?
js_156: Pick one thing you want to learn now and write ‘why’ in a single sentence. The purpose will pull the method along.
js_157: Am I only piling up input (reading, listening), or am I proving it with output (something I made)?
js_158: Turn one thing you learned this week into a short note, memo, or small result. Only by making it does your skill show.
js_159: Do I use AI as a lever for learning, or as a copier that just spits out answers?
js_160: Ask AI for the ‘explanation’ and the ‘why,’ not just the ‘answer.’ The power to question for yourself grows your self-study.
js_162: You’ve fully mastered the power to learn on your own in the AI age
